why: The May 1984 attack by the National Front for the Salvation of Libya targeted the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
The first political prisoners at Abu Salim arrived after the arrests that followed the May 1984 attack.
Abu Salim prison was built inside the Military Police Command compound.
Fighting in the Abu Salim district in 2011 centred on the area of the prison.
Rebel forces stormed the Bab al-Aziziya compound on 23 August 2011.
NATO air strikes in 2011 hit targets in and around the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
The April 1986 US air raid hit the Bab al-Aziziya barracks.

why: Military air base and civilian airport on one site.
During the May 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya, military police surrounded the building where the attackers had retreated and fighting lasted until early afternoon.

Public hangings were a response to opposition in 1984: after the May attack on Bab al-Aziziya, twelve of those involved were publicly hanged in their home towns, and further hangings were broadcast on state television.

why: Libya dismantled its centrifuge equipment at Al Hashan and, by April 2002, moved it to Al Fallah, where it stayed in storage.
Al Khalla succeeded Al Hashan as the centrifuge research and development site and was used to store uranium hexafluoride.
Libya moved the Japanese-supplied uranium conversion modules from Al Khalla to Salah Eddin for security and secrecy; IAEA inspectors first saw them there in December 2003.
US officials called the underground plant at Tarhuna "Rabta-II" because it appeared to be a copy of Rabta; Libya called it Pharma 300.
